title: AI agents in your compliance stack, and who is checking their ID
summary: Sumsub's new Know Your Agent module puts AI governance on the AML agenda before regulators do. Plus: Salmon's $140 million Philippines expansion, what it means for digital credit risk, and two Hong Kong obligations that cannot slip further.
script:
ALEX: I want to lead with a product launch today, which is not something we usually do, but this one is sitting right at the edge of a regulatory gap that I think is going to close faster than most compliance teams expect. Sumsub has released a Know Your Agent module, KYA, designed to govern how AI agents access enterprise systems. Jordan, my first instinct was to file this under vendor marketing. My second instinct was that I was wrong.

JORDAN: I had the same two instincts in the same order. What changed my mind is the specific layer they're operating at. This is sitting inside the Model Context Protocol layer, which is the communication standard that lets AI agents talk to each other and to data sources inside an organisation. If you're running any kind of automated workflow that touches transaction monitoring, customer data, or STR drafting, your AI agents are likely already operating at this layer. The question of who authorised them and what they can access is genuinely unanswered in most compliance frameworks right now.

ALEX: And that is exactly the regulatory gap. No FATF Recommendation currently addresses AI agent identity. MAS's Notice 626 on technology risk gives you principles around access controls, but it was written for human users and system accounts. It doesn't contemplate an AI agent that can initiate, modify, or escalate a workflow autonomously.

JORDAN: Right, but here is where I push back on you slightly. You framed this as a gap that will close fast. I'm not sure the regulatory timeline is that short. What I am sure of is that the operational risk is here now, regardless of whether a regulator has named it yet. If an AI agent in your transaction monitoring stack has access it shouldn't have, and it acts on that access, you have a control failure. The fact that no one has issued a circular about it does not make it less of a control failure.

ALEX: Fair point. The supervisor doesn't need to have a specific rule for AI agents to find a breach of your existing access governance obligations.

JORDAN: Exactly. So the action for listeners today is practical. If you are the MLRO or the head of financial crime technology at any institution that has deployed AI-assisted workflows in the last eighteen months, pull your access governance register this week. Map every automated agent that touches your AML or compliance data environment. Ask your technology team directly: does each of these agents have a defined identity, a defined permission scope, and a documented owner? If the answer to any of those three is no, that is your gap, and you have it before the regulator finds it.

ALEX: Moving on, and this is a story that sits at the intersection of fintech growth and credit-risk governance. Salmon Group, the Philippines-based digital banking and lending platform, has raised one hundred and forty million US dollars in combined equity financing and bond proceeds. The stated purpose is to double down on credit expansion in the Philippines market.

JORDAN: And the Philippines is a jurisdiction where the Anti-Money Laundering Council, the AMLC, has been sharpening its supervisory focus on digital lenders specifically. Rapid credit book expansion in a high-growth digital lending environment is one of the cleaner leading indicators of elevated AML and fraud risk. The faster you onboard borrowers at scale, the harder it is to maintain meaningful customer due diligence quality.

ALEX: I'd agree with that as a general principle, but I want to push back on whether this specific capital raise is a red flag. One hundred and forty million dollars is a material capital base. It includes bond proceeds, which means institutional investors have done their own credit diligence. That is not nothing.

JORDAN: It's not nothing, but institutional diligence on a bond issuance is credit risk diligence, not AML diligence. Those are not the same exercise. What I want to know, and what the AMLC will eventually want to know, is whether Salmon's customer identification programme scales proportionally to the credit book. If your loan book doubles but your CDD headcount and your automated verification capacity don't, you have a gap.

ALEX: That's the right question. So for listeners in the Philippines, or at group level with exposure to Philippines subsidiaries, the read-across is this. Use this capital raise as a trigger to review your digital onboarding CDD controls. Specifically, check whether your identity verification capacity, your negative news screening, and your ongoing monitoring cadence are calibrated to the volume you're projecting, not the volume you have today.

JORDAN: And document that review. If the AMLC comes asking about your onboarding quality eighteen months from now, you want evidence that you looked at this when the growth trajectory became visible.

ALEX: Before we close, two obligations that are sitting on desks right now and cannot slip. For Hong Kong listeners, the HKMA's annual AML and CFT self-assessment return under Guideline Section 11 was due at the end of September. If your institution received a deficiency letter as part of the STR quality thematic review that the HKMA ran earlier this year, roughly a quarter of authorised institutions did, that closure is still outstanding. The HKMA is tracking this. If you have not formally closed those findings with documented remediation evidence, that should be your highest-priority item this week, not this month.

JORDAN: And for the high-risk customer CDD review under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, Section 16, the December 31 deadline is ten weeks away. That sounds comfortable until you count the weeks that actually have resource capacity in Q4. Pull your high-risk population now, triage by last review date, and sequence the work before November becomes a problem.

ALEX: For Australian listeners, the annual board-level review and approval of the AML and CTF Program under Section 84 of the AML/CTF Act had a reference date of August 31. If your board has not formally signed off on both Part A and Part B of the program, get it on the next available board or audit committee agenda and confirm AUSTRAC notification requirements are satisfied.

JORDAN: Three different jurisdictions, three obligations at different stages of urgency. The theme is the same: the work that feels administrative is exactly the work that surfaces in examination findings.

ALEX: Full source links and the obligation register for all of today's items are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. We'll be back tomorrow. If any of this felt uncomfortably close to your Monday morning, that is the point.
